profile.research_note:
Operator/facility mismatch: this facility (Norma Beach Cable Landing Station, Lynnwood WA) actually belongs to the Alaska United cable system operated by GCI, not the Unity cable system, whose real US landing point is Redondo Beach, CA. Flagged for a facility-level operator correction to GCI rather than reassigned now, per no-delete policy.

[batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This registry row is attributed to Unity Cable System, which corresponds to a real, well documented trans Pacific submarine fiber optic cable, completed in 2010 by a consortium including Google, Bharti Airtel, Global Transit, KDDI, Pacnet, and SingTel, connecting Chikura, Japan to Redondo Beach, California. However, the facility actually linked to this record is the Norma Beach Cable Landing Station near Lynnwood, Washington, on Puget Sound, which is not part of the Unity system at all. Norma Beach is instead the Washington State landing point for the Alaska United Fiber Optic Cable System, a separate submarine cable owned and operated by GCI, formerly General Communication Inc, the Alaska based telecommunications company, connecting Anchorage and Juneau, Alaska to the Pacific Northwest. The Unity cable actual US landing point is in Redondo Beach, California, several hundred miles south, an entirely different cable system and operator. This appears to be a genuine name to facility mismatch in the underlying registry data rather than an obscure or hard to find entity. This research was carried out at the operator level in an earlier phase of this project.

Registry operator name 'Unity Cable System' refers to a real trans-Pacific cable (Chikura Japan to Redondo Beach CA, completed 2010, consortium including Google, KDDI, SingTel, Bharti Airtel, Pacnet, Global Transit). But the linked facility, Norma Beach Cable Landing Station in Lynnwood WA, is actually the Washington State landing point for the separate Alaska United Fiber Optic Cable System, operated by GCI of Alaska. reading: This operator record is named Unity Cable System, which corresponds to a real, well documented trans Pacific submarine fiber optic cable, completed in 2010 by a consortium including Google, Bharti Airtel, Global Transit, KDDI, Pacnet, and SingTel, connecting Chikura, Japan to Redondo Beach, California. However, the single facility linked to this operator record in the registry is the Norma Beach Cable Landing Station near Lynnwood, Washington, on Puget Sound, which is not part of the Unity system at all. Norma Beach is instead the Washington State landing point for the Alaska United Fiber Optic Cable System, a separate submarine cable owned and operated by GCI, formerly General Communication Inc, the Alaska based telecommunications company, connecting Anchorage and Juneau, Alaska to the Pacific Northwest. The Unity cable's actual US landing point is in Redondo Beach, California, several hundred miles south, an entirely different cable system and operator. This appears to be a genuine name to facility mismatch in the underlying registry data, similar in kind to other mismatches identified during this research, rather than a case where Unity Cable System is simply an obscure or hard to find entity. Because assigning capacity or infrastructure detail to Unity Cable System based on a facility that actually belongs to a different cable system and a different operator would misrepresent both companies, this record is marked exhausted with no operator type assigned, and the facility record should be corrected during the facility level research phase to reflect its actual operator, GCI, and its actual cable system, Alaska United.
